questions.question: Explain why comparing the dew point to the air temperature is more useful than reading either number alone.
questions.expected_answer: The gap between them measures how close the air is to saturation. A small gap (18 °C vs 16 °C) means the air needs to cool only slightly for condensation — humid air with cloud, mist or rain likely. A large gap means dry air. Either number alone gives temperature information but not moisture status.

questions.question: Describe how you would confirm that a line on the chart really is the cold front, using evidence from stations on both sides of it.
questions.expected_answer: Check the symbol (triangles pointing in the direction of movement), then verify the air masses: ahead of the front stations should show warm, humid north-westerly flow with increasing cloud; behind it stations should show colder temperatures, south-westerly winds, rising pressure and showers. Kinked isobars crossing the line add further confirmation.

questions.question: In your own words, explain why the weather changes so sharply when a cold front passes — what is physically happening to the two air masses?
questions.expected_answer: A cold front is the boundary where dense cold air wedges under lighter warm air and lifts it rapidly. The forced ascent creates cumulonimbus and heavy showers at the line. Once the front passes, the warm air has been displaced aloft and replaced by cold air at the surface — so temperature drops, wind swings to south-westerly, pressure rises, and showers give way to clearing skies.
